cards.text: This poem comes from a man who says he has "seen affliction under the rod of God's wrath". For twenty verses he pours out his pain, and he even says his hope from the LORD has perished. Then, right in the middle of all that dark, he says, "Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope:"

cards.question: The man is about to say what he calls to mind, the thing that gives him hope. What does he say is the reason we are not consumed?

answers.text: The loving devotion of the LORD
The strength of the city walls

cards.text: His mercies never fail, and they are new EVERY MORNING. Friend, in the junk drawer the only thing new every morning was a fresh layer of the same old dust.

cards.question: The poet cries out, "great is Your faithfulness!" True or false: he's saying it to his people.

cards.text: Now his own soul jumps in with something to say about the LORD. Twenty verses of pain, and the soul is the one grabbing the mic.

cards.question: "The LORD is my portion," says my soul, "therefore I will ___ in Him."

cards.text: This isn't only about him anymore. Now the poet tells us what the LORD is like toward people.

cards.question: The poet says the LORD is good to the soul who seeks Him. Who else does he say the LORD is good to?
True or false: the poet says it is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD.

cards.text: Waiting QUIETLY, which the dead batteries I shared that drawer with could never once pull off. Next the poet says it is good for a man to bear the yoke while he is still young.

cards.question: The poet says the man under that yoke should sit alone in silence. Who does he say laid the yoke on him?

cards.text: Let him bury his face in the dust, offer his cheek to the one who would strike him, and be filled with reproach. Heavy stuff, friend.

cards.question: True or false: with his face in the dust, the poet says all hope is gone.
Right after the dust and the strikes and the reproach, the poet gives a reason. What is it?

answers.text: The Lord will not cast us off forever
The hard times will soon be forgotten
The people will rise up again soon

cards.text: Then the poet faces the hard part head on. He says even if the Lord causes grief, that isn't the end of it.

cards.question: Even if He causes grief, He will show ___ according to His abundant loving devotion.
True or false: the poet says the Lord willingly afflicts and grieves the sons of men.

cards.text: Then the poet names three things: crushing all the prisoners of the land underfoot, denying a man justice before the Most High, and twisting a man's lawsuit.

cards.question: True or false: the Lord approves of denying a man justice.

cards.text: Now the poet asks who has spoken and it came to pass. Friend, I have told my oven HURRY UP a hundred times, and not once has it come to pass.

cards.question: The poet asks who can speak and see it come to pass, unless someone has ordained it. Who?
Do not both ___ and ___ come from the mouth of the Most High?

cards.text: The poet's last question is about complaining. The expired coupon I shared that drawer with never complained once, and friend, it was EXPIRED.

cards.question: The poet asks why any mortal man should complain, in view of what?

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 6 quotes "therefore I will ___ in Him.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Lamentations 3:25 says the LORD is good 'to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him.' These two lines run side by side, and the text doesn't say whether they are the same people or two groups. Asking 'Who else does he say the LORD is good to?' treats them as two separate groups, which settles something the text leaves open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The joke says the dead batteries 'could never once pull off' waiting quietly. That only works if the baker knows the batteries argued all the time, and that detail was never set up for the baker. On its own, a dead battery is silent, so a stranger would say 'huh?'

rule.text: It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining. If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it. A callback only works if its setup came earlier in this lesson or conversation.

findings.problem: The statement 'the Lord approves of denying a man justice' depends on two verses. 'Denying a man justice' is in 3:35, and 'of these the Lord does not approve' is in 3:36. The card cites only Lamentations 3:36 and should cite Lamentations 3:35-36.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower. A choice card cites only the verses of its right answer.

findings.problem: This card fills in the blanks of a quoted line, 'Do not both ___ and ___ come from the mouth of the Most High?', and no story card sets up 3:38. Even a baker who reasons that the pair is good and adversity has to guess the order, since 'adversity' must go first. Getting the card right comes down to guessing the wording and its order, not to understanding the verse.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: The question is 'The poet asks who can speak and see it come to pass, unless someone has ordained it. Who?' The final 'Who?' could mean the one who speaks or the one who ordains. The intended answer, 'The Lord', is the one who ordains. Read the first way, the honest answer to the rhetorical question would be 'no one'.
findings.question: The docs have no rule about a question being unclear about what it asks. Should a rule be added, and should this card be reworded, for example to 'Who does the poet say must ordain it?'
